title: The Letter to Philemon
subtitle: Pros Philēmona, “To Philemon”
description: Paul’s shortest letter, and his most personal: a prisoner’s appeal to a friend about a slave. Onesimus has wronged his master Philemon, met Paul in chains, and become a Christian, and now Paul sends him home with this letter in his hand. With great tact and warmth Paul asks Philemon to take him back “no longer as a slave but as more than a slave, a dear brother”, to welcome him as he would welcome Paul himself, and to put anything he owes on Paul’s account. A letter that can be read in five minutes, and that has asked every generation of the church what the gospel does to the walls between people. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to Philemon?
qa.answer: The eighteenth book of the New Testament and the shortest of Paul’s letters, a single chapter of twenty-five verses. Paul writes from prison to Philemon, a believer in whose home a church met, probably at Colossae, on behalf of Onesimus, Philemon’s slave, who had become a Christian through Paul. He asks Philemon to receive Onesimus back as a dear brother in the Lord (verse 16).

qa.question: Who wrote Philemon, and when?
qa.answer: The apostle Paul, writing with Timothy (verse 1), and almost all scholars agree that the letter is his. He was a prisoner at the time (verses 1, 9), and the letter was carried together with Colossians, which names the same companions and says Onesimus was travelling with Tychicus (Colossians 4:7–9). It is usually dated to Paul’s imprisonment in Rome around AD 60–62, though some scholars place it during an earlier imprisonment at Ephesus.

qa.question: Was Onesimus a runaway slave?
qa.answer: The traditional reading is that he ran away from Philemon, perhaps having stolen from him (verse 18), and met Paul by God’s providence. Some scholars think instead that he went to Paul on purpose after a quarrel, to ask him to plead with his master, which Roman law did not count as running away. Either way, Paul says he was “parted from you for a little while” (verse 15) and sends him back with this letter, asking that he be received as Paul himself would be.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
